q: Saturday, 16:30, light wind. The technician ticks 'Sails: OK' and says they were checked yesterday. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: The main hoisted and the genoa unrolled now, while it is calm
o: Nothing — it was checked yesterday and the form says OK
A look inside the stackpack and the sail bags, unhoisted
To unroll them yourself on the first morning and phone in faults
why: Sails are checked hoisted: at the pontoon in light wind, not at sea; a faulty sail found on Sunday is your problem.

fig.title: Check-in form — sails
lines: Checked yesterday — technician
Wind at the pontoon: F2, no swell
Main in the stackpack, genoa furled

q: The genoa is fully unrolled. You look at the furling drum and see this. What do you ask for?
a: The line rewound tight on the drum with the sail fully out
o: Nothing — the drum should be empty when the sail is out
Three turns taken off the drum so the sail unrolls fully
The slack on deck coiled, tied off to the pulpit and left
why: With the sail fully out the drum must hold enough line to roll it all in; one turn left means the line runs out mid-furl.

fig.note: Genoa fully out · rest of the line slack on deck

q: Halfway through furling the genoa the line goes solid. The technician reaches for a winch handle. You look up and see this. What do you do?
a: Stop him — unroll, clear the wrap, and have the base fix the halyard lead
o: Let him winch it — a halyard wrap pulls itself out once under load
Sheet the genoa in hard on the winch to drag the wrap down the foil
Note 'stiff furler' on the form and grease the swivel yourself once at sea
why: A halyard wrap jams the swivel; winching it damages the foil and the halyard. The halyard angle at the masthead is the base's job.

fig.title: Genoa furler — jammed
lines: Halyard wound twice round the forestay above the swivel
Furling line: solid, two turns on the drum
Technician: 'always stiff — winch it'

q: The technician runs the genoa sheet through the car for you. You check the car itself and see this. What do you ask for?
a: The plunger pin replaced so the car locks in the track
o: Nothing — the cord lashing holds the car where it is
The port car moved across to starboard; one car is enough
A shackle through the car to the toe rail once at sea
why: A car that is not pinned slides under load: the sheet lead goes and the car can hit the end stop; the pin is a base fix.

fig.note: Starboard car lashed to the track with cord · port car OK

q: The genoa is out. You walk the leech and see this. What do you do?
a: Photograph both, note them on the form, ask for the strip restitched today
o: Nothing — the UV strip is cosmetic and a leech line is only a trim aid
Tape the strip down and tie off the leech line yourself, then move on
Sign now and mention both at check-out if they have got any worse
why: A loose UV strip tears off and takes stitching with it; the leech line flogs the leech. Both are quick fixes at the base, not at sea.

fig.title: Genoa leech
lines: UV strip: stitching gone along 1.5 m, strip hanging
Leech line: cleat at the clew broken, line flapping
Cloth under the strip: sound

q: At the genoa clew you find this. The technician says it has sailed like that all season. What do you do?
a: Insist the base repairs the clew now — it carries the whole sheet load
o: Accept it — two of the three loops are still holding the ring
Tie the sheets to the ring with a round turn and two half hitches instead
Note it on the form and ask for a reduced deposit for the week
why: A clew lets go in a gust and the sail flogs itself to pieces; a chafed clew is the base's repair, not a note.

fig.title: Genoa clew
lines: Clew ring: webbing, 3 loops
One loop chafed through, one frayed
Sheets tied with bowlines, no shackle

q: The main goes up at the pontoon and you see this. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: Battens and the slide replaced now; the zip photographed and on the form
o: Everything on the form — you will be sailing on reef 1 most days anyway
A spare batten and a spare slide to fit yourself at the first anchorage
The zip fixed now; battens only matter with the full main up
why: Missing battens let the leech flog and tear; a cracked slide jams the hoist. The zip only keeps the cover shut.

fig.title: Mainsail hoisted
lines: Batten 2 (from the top): pocket empty
Batten 3: snapped, bends in the middle
One luff slide cracked; stackpack zip slider missing

q: You run the genoa sheets to the winches and look at them. What do you ask for?
a: The port sheet replaced and the second spare line found before you sign
o: The port sheet end-for-ended so the chafe sits at the tail end
Nothing — a sheet lasts the week; the spare takes over if it goes
Both sheets swapped for the spare lines and the old sheets noted on the form
why: A bare core fails under load and a 14 m sheet will not reach the winch on a wide genoa; spares are counted, not assumed.

fig.note: Port 14 m · starboard 16 m · spare lines: list 2, found 1

q: The boat has in-mast furling. The technician asks you to unfurl the main yourself. How do you do it?
a: Outhaul out on the winch, the furling line eased with a little tension kept on
o: Furling line cast off fully first, then the outhaul hauled out on the winch
Furling line and outhaul hauled together so the roll stays tight
Outhaul winched out with the furling line still shut in its clutch
why: The roll must stay firm as it leaves the mast: slack on the furling line lets it bunch and jam in the slot; never winch against a closed clutch.

fig.note: In-mast main · outhaul on the winch, furling line in a clutch

q: Now the technician furls the main back in. You watch the boom and the lines. What do you ask him to change?
a: Boom up to the base's mark on the topping lift, a little outhaul tension kept
o: Boom lower still on the topping lift so the sail drops into the mast on its own
Outhaul let fully go so that nothing at all resists the roll into the mast
Furling line pulled faster, two hands, so the roll stays tight in the mast
why: The boom at the set angle feeds the luff square into the slot; a loose roll creases and jams, and a jammed furler is never forced.

fig.title: In-mast main — furling in
lines: Topping lift eased: boom end below horizontal
Outhaul: slack
Furling line pulled fast, by hand

q: The technician points at the clutches and says 'reefs are there'. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: Reef 1 put in at the pontoon, so you see which line does what and runs free
o: The colour code written on the form so you can look it up when you need it
A spare clutch handed over in case one of the reef clutches fails at sea
The reef lines coiled and stowed below; you will try them out at sea
why: A reef is practised at the pontoon in calm, not worked out at 25 knots; a jammed reef line is then the base's fix.

fig.title: Clutches — port coachroof
lines: Red: main halyard
Blue: reef 1 · blue/white: reef 2
White: outhaul · black: kicker

q: You look at the gooseneck and the reef lines. What does this tell you about reefing at sea?
a: Two-line: the luff cringle is hooked on a horn at the mast, then the clew line hauled
o: Single-line: one pull from the cockpit reefs both the luff and the clew together
The horns take the tack only; the reefs are single-line, pulled from the cockpit
The luff reefs with the halyard alone; the horns are spare fittings, unused
why: Horns at the gooseneck mean the luff is hooked by hand: plan who goes forward, clipped on, before you need a reef.

fig.title: Reefing gear
lines: Cockpit: one line per reef, to the clew cringle
Gooseneck: two horns (hooks)
Luff cringles: free, no line

q: The main is sheeted in at the pontoon and you see this. What do you settle with the base before you sign?
a: Whether the bimini folds under sail or the boom is held clear — and who pays if it tears
o: Nothing — it is only canvas; the boom slides over it on a gybe without harm
The bimini taken off and left ashore at the base for the week, fitted again on Friday
The boom held up high on the topping lift and cleated there for the whole week
why: A boom that meets the bimini on a gybe tears it, and the damage comes off your deposit; agree the rule now, in writing on the form.

fig.title: Boom & bimini
lines: Main sheeted in: boom end 3 cm above the bimini frame
Bimini: folds aft in a minute
Technician: 'everyone sails like that'

q: The genoa is out in F2 and the luff looks like this. The technician says it always does. What do you do?
a: Tension the halyard until the scallops just go, then check the furler still turns
o: Leave it — a slack luff rolls up tighter on the furler and sets better
Winch the halyard bar-tight; a furling genoa can never be too tight
Ease the backstay a turn — the scallops come from forestay sag, not from the halyard
why: Scallops mean a slack luff; set the halyard so they disappear, no more — an over-tight halyard stiffens the furler and wraps.

fig.title: Genoa luff
lines: Horizontal scallops along the luff
Furler turns freely by hand
Genoa halyard: in a clutch at the mast

q: Your check of the mainsheet, traveller and vang gives this list. What goes to the base to fix now, and what on the form?
a: The cracked block replaced now; the chafed cover photographed and on the form
o: Everything on the form — nothing has actually failed yet, so nothing to fix
Both replaced now before you sign, or you do not take the boat at all
The chafed line replaced now, the block noted — rope fails before metal
why: A cracked block under mainsheet load can burst and hurt someone: repair now. A chafed cover on a sound core: note it, watch it.

fig.title: Mainsheet, traveller, vang
lines: Mainsheet lower block: one cheek cracked
Traveller control line: cover chafed, core sound
Vang: 8:1, cleat holds

q: The inventory lists a preventer. You find this in the cockpit locker. What do you ask for?
a: A line long enough from the boom end to the bow and back to a cockpit winch
o: Nothing — 6 m from the boom end to the toe rail amidships is how it is rigged
A boom brake instead of it; a preventer line is only for racing boats
A second 6 m line so you can rig one on each side at the same time
why: A preventer runs from the boom end forward to the bow and back aft, so it can be eased from the cockpit; a short strop to the rail breaks the boom.

fig.title: Inventory — deck
lines: Preventer line: 1 — found: 6 m, snap hook
Boom end: pad eye fitted
Bow: cleat and fairlead

q: The inventory lists the sails below. You open the forepeak. What do you do before you sign?
a: Have the storm jib found or struck off the list, and the count on the form
o: Sign — you will not fly a storm jib in August in the Ionian anyway
Take the technician's word that it is in the office and will be put back
Count the bags, not the contents: two bags on the list, two bags found
why: What is on the signed list is what you hand back on Friday; a sail you never had is charged against your deposit.

fig.title: Inventory — sails
lines: Gennaker with sock: 1
Storm jib: 1
Found: bag 'Gennaker' (sail + sock); bag 'Storm jib' — empty

q: Sunday, your first sail. Off the headland the genoa furling line goes solid with the sail half rolled. What do you do?
a: Ease the sheet, try again by hand, and call the base for instructions — cut nothing
o: Put the furling line on the electric winch and grind the sail in, turn by turn
Cut the furling line at the drum and roll the sail by hand round the foil
Leave it half out, hoist the main and carry on under both to the anchorage
why: A jammed furler is a base problem: forcing or cutting it turns a phone call into a damaged foil and a deposit claim.

fig.title: Day 1 — off Lefkas
lines: Genoa half rolled, furling line solid
Wind 20 kn and rising
Base: 40 min away under engine

q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician says 'the main goes up like on any boat'. You look at the lazy bag and the head of the sail. What do you ask to see?
a: The main hoisted and dropped once: how the square top goes into the bag, and where you zip it
o: Only the sail number on the bag — a catamaran's main hoists like any other mainsail does
That the bag can stay zipped shut and the main hoisted straight up through it
A ladder added to the inventory so you can reach the zip from the deck at anchor
why: A square top with two headboard cars needs the lazyjacks and the bag opened right, at a height; see it done once at the pontoon.

fig.title: Catamaran mainsail
lines: Square-top main: headboard on two cars
Lazy bag zip: 2.6 m above the coachroof
Boom reached from the coachroof steps

q: At the briefing you are given this. What does it mean for your week?
a: Reef at those numbers and stay in port above F6 — they are contract terms, not advice
o: Reef when the boat feels overpressed; the numbers are a guide for beginners
The limit is for the forecast only; at sea you carry on as you judge best
The reef numbers apply only with the full genoa out; with the main alone they do not
why: Sailing above the contract limit, or unreefed when told to reef, can void the insurance and put the damage on you.

fig.title: Contract & briefing — wind
lines: Sailing permitted up to F6 on the base forecast
Reef 1 at 18 kn, reef 2 at 25 kn
Above F6: stay in port, call the base

q: You follow the genoa furling line from the drum aft along the side deck and find this. What do you ask for?
a: A lead block fitted at the gap so the line runs fair, not over the stanchion base
o: Nothing — the line only touches the base while the sail is fully out
The line lashed to that stanchion with a short cord so it cannot move
A spare furling line put aboard in case this one chafes through
why: A furling line chafing on a stanchion base jams or parts mid-furl; the lead blocks are the base's fittings, counted like the rest.

fig.note: Furling line, drum to cockpit · list: 4 blocks, fitted: 3

q: Reading the inventory again, you compare it with the number on the genoa's clew. What do you do before you sign?
a: Have the form corrected to the number on the sail — that is the sail you hand back
o: Nothing — the base swaps sails between boats and the form is only indicative
Write the main's number on the genoa clew with a marker so the two agree
Ask for the genoa with the number on the form to be fitted instead of this one
why: On Friday the inventory is checked by number: a sail listed wrongly is 'missing' and charged against your deposit.

fig.title: Inventory — sails
lines: Main: no. 4512 · Genoa: no. 4512
On the genoa clew: no. 3870
Technician: 'they get swapped around'

q: On the hoist the technician stops winching at this point. Your crew ask what the tape is for. What do you tell them?
a: It marks full hoist: stop there, or the headboard jams against the masthead sheave
o: It marks a worn spot on the halyard; move the tape when the chafe moves
It marks reef 1: the sail is lowered to the tape for the first reef
It is the base's inventory tag; the lines are counted by their tapes
why: A halyard winched past its mark drives the headboard into the sheave: the halyard stretches, the sail will not come down.

fig.note: Main at full hoist · black tape 5 cm short of the clutch

q: Your crew are already planning a gennaker day. At the briefing you read this clause. What does it mean for the week?
a: Ask for the base's written OK now, keep to 12 kn and daylight — a torn gennaker is paid in full
o: Fly it whenever the wind allows; the clause is advice to keep beginners off it
Fly it only after raising the deposit to cover it; the base adjusts the hold
Leave it in the bag all week; a gennaker on a charter boat is never for the crew
why: The gennaker is usually outside the damage waiver: the clause sets who, when and the limit, and you carry the whole repair bill.

fig.title: Contract — gennaker
lines: Use only with the base's written OK
Max 12 kn true, daylight, sock rigged
Damage to it: not covered by the waiver

q: Your crew ask where the topping lift is before the main comes down. You look at the boom and see this. What do you tell them?
a: There is none: the rigid vang holds the boom up with the sail down — just ease the mainsheet
o: Rig the spare halyard to the boom end as a lift every time before the drop
Pull the vang control line on hard before the drop so the boom cannot fall
Hold the boom up by hand at the drop; without a lift it falls on the bimini
why: A gas-strut vang replaces the topping lift: it carries the boom when the halyard is let go; a strut that sags is a base repair.

fig.title: Boom support
lines: Rigid vang with gas strut
Topping lift: none fitted
Mainsheet eased, main down: boom stays up

q: The main halyard goes to an electric winch. The technician shows you the button. What rule do you give the crew?
a: Short pushes, eyes on the sail, stop at any snag — never hold the button against a load
o: Hold the button until the winch stalls; the motor's cut-out protects the sail
Only the skipper touches the button; the crew hoist by hand with the handle
Use the button only for the last metre; the first part is hoisted by hand
why: An electric winch does not feel a snag: a batten in a lazyjack or a jammed slide tears before the motor notices.

fig.note: Push-button at the coachroof · two speeds · halyard 10 mm

q: The technician hands you the furling line to roll the genoa in. It takes everything you have, though there is no wrap aloft. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to check the drum and swivel bearings now — in F2 a furler rolls in by hand
o: Lead the line to the electric winch and roll it in on the button
Spray the drum and swivel with lubricant yourself and sign
Note 'stiff furler' and furl the genoa only in light winds this week
why: A furler that needs the winch at the pontoon will not furl at all at 25 kn; bearings are the base's job and no amount of spray fixes them.

fig.title: Genoa furler
lines: Sail fully out, sheet eased, F2
Rolls in by hand: barely, with both hands
Masthead by binoculars: no halyard wrap

q: The genoa is out in F2 and looks like this. The form says it is fine. What do you do?
a: Photograph luff and leech, write 'genoa: aged, stretched' on the form, and plan to reef it early
o: Demand a new genoa before you sign; the contract promises sails in good condition
Nothing — the age of the cloth is not something the check-in form records
Ask for a lower deposit for the week since the sail is likely to blow out
why: An old sail is not damage the base repairs, but its state goes on the form so a blow-out this week is not charged as new; sail it conservatively.

fig.title: Genoa in F2
lines: Cloth stiff and crackly, UV strip faded
Draft well aft, leech hooked
Form: 'Genoa — 2019 — OK'

q: Main hoisted, you walk the leech from the cockpit and spot this. The technician points at the locker. What do you do?
a: The tear sewn or patched by the base's sailmaker before departure, and written on the form
o: Tape it on both sides yourself; a tear this size does not grow in the Ionian
Note it and keep reef 2 in all week so that part of the leech stays rolled away
Nothing — a tear that small is within normal wear for a charter sail
why: A tear at the leech grows with every flog; sail tape is a sea-going stopgap, and a tear you accept unrepaired is yours at check-out.

fig.title: Mainsail hoisted
lines: Tear 10 cm at the leech, above batten 3 pocket
Cloth around it: sound
Technician: 'sail tape is in the locker'

q: Hoisting the main at the pontoon, your crew member on the winch feels it stop and asks whether to keep winching. You look up and see this. What do you say?
a: Stop — ease a little so the batten drops clear of the lazyjack, then hoist again by hand
o: Keep winching — the batten end pops through once the halyard is tight
Let the lazyjacks go altogether; they only get in the way of the hoist
Drop the main, pull all the battens out, hoist it and refit them aloft
why: A batten end winched against a lazyjack tears the pocket; slack the lazyjacks forward or head to wind, and hoist with eyes aloft.

fig.note: Hoist stops at two-thirds · lazyjack across the batten pocket

q: The 36 ft boat is simpler than your last charter. You read its sail handling on the form. What does this change for Thursday evening, coming into the bay?
a: Someone clipped on at the mast to flake the main onto the boom as it drops, head to wind under engine, before the bay
o: Nothing — the main drops onto the boom and into the cover like a stackpack
Drop the main in the bay once the anchor is down; the sail flakes itself
Keep the main up until the anchor is set; it steadies the boat in the bay
why: Without lazyjacks the dropped main falls over the deck and the helm's view: plan the drop outside, with a crew member at the mast.

fig.title: 36 ft — mainsail
lines: Slab reefing at the mast, no lazyjacks, no stackpack
Sail cover with ties
Halyard and reef lines at the mast

q: You unclip the main halyard from the headboard to look at it. What do you ask for?
a: The shackle replaced before you sign — one that opens drops the main and sends the halyard aloft
o: A second cable tie through the pin and a line on the form
Nothing — the headboard cars hold the sail if the shackle lets go
The halyard tied to the headboard with a bowline instead of the shackle
why: A halyard shackle carries the whole luff load: a stripped pin held by plastic is a failure waiting for a gust, and a lost halyard ends the week.

fig.title: Main halyard shackle
lines: Captive-pin shackle: thread stripped
Pin held by a cable tie
Technician: 'it has held all season'

q: You take the binoculars to the masthead before the main goes up and see this. What do you ask for?
a: The base sends someone up the mast to clear it now — a crossed halyard is a mast job
o: Hoist the main anyway: the last metre comes with the halyard winched hard
Tie the spare halyard off at the bow and live with the crossed lines
Go up in the bosun's chair yourself with the technician on the winch
why: Halyards crossed above the sheaves chafe through each other and stop the hoist short; it is cleared from aloft, by the base, before you leave.

fig.title: Masthead by binoculars

Main stops 1 m short of full hoist
Spare halyard: wrapped round the forestay

q: Main sheeted in at the pontoon, you load the mainsheet by hand and the tail creeps through the cleat. What do you ask for?
a: The cam cleat replaced before you sign — a mainsheet that will not hold cannot be trusted on a gybe
o: Lead the mainsheet to the genoa winch instead for the week
A figure-of-eight in the tail behind the cleat so it cannot run out
A note on the form; it only slips above twenty knots anyway
why: The mainsheet must hold on its own cleat under full load; worn cam teeth let the boom out in a gust, with crew in the way.

q: Your crew ask what the fitting under the boom is and whether a preventer is still needed. What do you tell them?
a: A boom brake: set its line before a downwind leg so the boom crosses slowly — it slows a gybe, it does not stop one
o: A boom brake: it locks the boom like a preventer, so no preventer is needed
A second vang: pull it on hard upwind and leave it slack on a run
A dinghy-hoist fitting; nothing to do with the boom under sail
why: A brake lets the boom come across under friction on a gybe; it never pins the boom, so an accidental gybe still happens, only slower.

Preventer line: 1 on the list

a: The gennaker hoisted in its sock at the pontoon, sock raised a metre and lowered, tack line and halyard found
o: Nothing — a gennaker is checked by flying it on the first downwind leg
The sail pulled out of the bag on the pontoon and looked over for tears
The sock taken off; a gennaker without a sock is simpler for a crew

Tack line, gennaker halyard: on the list, not found
Tack fitting: ring on the bow roller

o: Nothing — patches are there to be worn through; that is their job
Sail tape over the patches, and a note on the form
The spreader tips taped instead; then the sail needs no patches

Autopilot in wind mode so it follows every shift while you hoist
Sail out on the genoa and hoist the main outside, running downwind

o: A note 'sticky slides' and a crew member at the mast for every drop
Nothing — a main always needs a hand on the luff to come down
Silicone spray on the track yourself before you sign

o: Accept it — reef 1 and a rolled genoa is reefed enough for F6
Tie an extension onto the tail with a sheet bend and note it
Take the line out and keep it as a spare sheet; reef 2 is for storms

o: Nothing — a self-tacker has no sheets, cars or leads to go wrong
That the overlapping genoa from the forepeak is bent on instead; it is faster
That the car is lashed in the middle of the track so it cannot move

q: Thursday, 14:00, 22 kn on a beam reach. Your crew member says they will put the furling line on the winch. What do you say?
a: Bear away to blanket the genoa behind the main, ease the sheet but keep a little on it, and haul the line by hand
o: Winch it in on the beam reach with the sheet cleated — the winch has the power
Luff head to wind and let the sail flog while the line is hauled
Drop the genoa on deck instead; a furler is not meant for 22 knots

Sheet: cleated hard on the winch
Crew: 'I'll put the line on the winch'

q: Monday, 08:00, in a bay. The base's forecast is on your phone; your crew say you will reef when it gets strong. What do you do?
a: Put reef 1 in at the hoist, still at anchor, and shake it out later if the wind never comes
o: Hoist full and reef when the first gust arrives; reefing early wastes a nice morning
Stay at anchor until the base calls to say the wind has dropped
Leave the main in the bag and motor all day; the contract numbers are for sailing
why: A reef is put in at the hoist, in the flat water, when the forecast says it will be needed; shaking one out is easy, reefing late is not.

fig.title: Monday — in the bay
lines: Base forecast: NW 18–22 kn by noon
Contract: reef 1 at 18 kn, reef 2 at 25 kn
Now in the bay: 6 kn

q: You watch the technician furl the genoa away at the end of the check and see this. What do you ask for?
a: The sail unrolled and furled the other way so the UV strip is outside — and ask which way the drum turns
o: Nothing — the strip only matters while the sail is stored ashore
The strip pulled out and over the roll by hand without unrolling
A cover made to fit over the furled genoa for the week
why: The UV strip protects the roll only on the outside; furled the wrong way the sail cooks all week and the sheets wrap in the wrong direction.

fig.title: Genoa furled
lines: UV strip: inside the roll, white cloth outside
Sheets: 3 turns round the sail
Furling line: full on the drum

q: Thursday, 16:00, in harbour 25 miles from the base. The base's forecast arrives. What do you do?
a: Leave now or at first light, reefed, and tell the base your plan — Friday at 10:00 would be above the limit
o: Stay and leave Friday at 10:00 as planned; F6 is within the contract limit
Stay put and let the base fetch the boat; the limit means you may not sail
Leave Friday at 06:00 under full sail to be fast ahead of the wind
why: The limit is read against the forecast for the passage: sailing into a forecast F6–7 breaks the contract, so the passage moves to before it.

fig.title: Thursday — base forecast
lines: Friday from 10:00: NW F6, gusts F7
Tonight and early morning: NW 10–14 kn
Base: 25 M, about 5 h · boat due Friday 17:00

q: Tuesday, 15 kn, furling the main in. The line goes solid at halfway and your crew member on the electric winch says 'one more push'. What do you do?
a: Stop the winch, unroll a turn to clear the bunch, boom to its mark, then furl again by hand with outhaul tension
o: Hold the button — the winch has the power to pull the bunch through the slot
Drop the boom further so the sail hangs slack and pulls itself into the mast
Leave the main half furled, sheet it in hard and motor to the bay
why: A bunch in the slot only gets tighter under power; back off a turn and feed the roll in square, the way it was shown at the pontoon.

fig.title: Tuesday — furling the main
lines: Furling line solid at half; cloth bunched at the slot
Boom: below the mark on the topping lift
Crew on the electric winch: 'one more push'

q: Wednesday, 17:00, at anchor. Your crew admit the gennaker tore in a broach and suggest bagging it quietly. What do you do?
a: Call the base today, photograph it, and have it noted — hiding it costs more at check-out than the repair
o: Bag it and say nothing; the inventory counts bags, not the state of the sail
Patch it with sail tape and fly it again so the tear looks like old wear
Report it on Friday at check-out, when the technician asks about the sails
why: The contract says damage is reported at once; a tear found by the base after a cover-up loses you the waiver's goodwill and the whole deposit.

fig.title: Wednesday — at anchor
lines: Gennaker: 2 m tear along the foot after a broach
Crew: 'bag it, nobody looks inside'
Contract: damage reported at once; gennaker outside the waiver

q: Kos, Saturday. Trying reef 2 you find this, and the base's forecast is on the board. The technician shrugs. What do you do?
a: A sailmaker's repair before departure or another boat — with a Meltemi forecast reef 2 is the reef you will use
o: Accept it with a note on the form; reef 1 and a scrap of genoa will do for F6
Tie a strop through the cloth round the boom as a makeshift reef 2 and sign
Postpone departure to Monday and let the base decide what to do then
why: A torn cringle cannot take a reef load; in the Dodecanese in a Meltemi week you will sail on reef 2 most days, so it is fixed or the boat is not fit.

fig.title: Reef 2 cringle
lines: Clew cringle reef 2: ring torn half out of the leech
Base forecast Wed–Thu: N F6–7 (Meltemi)
Technician: 'nobody uses reef 2 in August'

q: The boat has in-mast furling and it is blowing F4 at the pontoon. The technician will not unfurl the main today. What do you do?
a: Have it rolled out a metre and back to prove it runs, and write 'main not fully seen at check-in' on the form
o: Sign — an in-mast main cannot be checked at a pontoon in any case
Insist on the whole main out in F4 at the pontoon; it is your right
Unfurl it yourself at the first anchorage and photograph any fault for the base
why: You sign for what you were shown: a short test proves the furler turns, and the note means a fault found on Sunday is not your fault.

fig.title: Saturday — pontoon
lines: In-mast main, F4 across the pontoon
Technician: 'not in this wind, it's fine'
Form: 'Sails: checked — OK'

q: Thursday, 13:00, Meltemi 25 kn. Reef 2 is in and the genoa is half rolled; your crew say it is fine. You look forward and see this. What do you do?
a: Move the cars forward for the smaller sail and roll a little more — a flogging half genoa wears itself out in an hour
o: Leave it — with reef 2 in, the main does the work and the genoa hardly matters
Unroll the genoa fully so the leech stops flogging, and ease the main
Roll the genoa away and motor-sail on the main alone to stay within the limit
why: A reefed genoa needs its lead moved forward or the leech flogs; a flogging leech shreds the UV strip and stitching — damage you pay for.
